You express a concession (Obwohl die Bäume krank sind, …; Sie sind krank. Trotzdem …; Auch wenn …) and take the floor in a public discussion: Ich möchte etwas ergänzen…

Use “obwohl” + a clause with the verb at the end (Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir).
Use “trotzdem / dennoch” as an adverb, with the verb in 2nd position (Es regnet. Trotzdem gehen wir).
Use “auch wenn / selbst wenn” for hypothetical concessions.
Take the floor, interrupt and respond politely in a discussion.

It's March 2032. The district council wants to fell six old chestnut trees on Kastanienallee to build a step-free tram stop. A residents' meeting is taking place in the school hall. Mrs Krause from the council is speaking.

Ladies and gentlemen, the six chestnut trees in front of the stop have to be felled. Although we regret this, we have no other choice. The trees are infested with the leaf miner moth, and the roots are lifting the pavement.
May I say something? I drove trams for forty years. I know how important a step-free stop is. Even so, I'm against the felling.
Mr Brandt, your objection is justified. But the trees are diseased. Even if we treat them, they'll live ten more years at most.
Maybe I'll only live ten more years too. Even so, nobody's felling me.

Sorry to interrupt. I'm a teacher at the school here. May I add something? The children walk to school under these trees every day. Although the trees are diseased, every autumn they collect conkers under them.
I understand that. Nevertheless, safety is more important. Last winter a big branch fell on a parked car.
I'd have a suggestion. Even if the old trees have to go, we could plant new ones. Not just any trees, but chestnut trees from our street.
From your street? What do you mean?
In the courtyard of number thirty-one there's a healthy chestnut tree, more than a hundred years old. The children could plant its conkers in the autumn. In two years we'd have young trees.
That would be a wonderful school project. Even if it takes longer.
I have to admit, I like it. Let's vote. Who is in favour of this proposal?
“das Wort ergreifen” = to take the floor
“op-VOHL”: final b sounds like “p”, stress on the second syllable.
“obwohl” introduces a subordinate clause: the conjugated verb goes to the END.
They go for a walk, although it's raining.
When the “obwohl” clause comes first, the main clause starts with the verb: “Obwohl es regnet, GEHEN wir.”
“trotzdem” links two main clauses. After it, the verb comes in 2nd position:
Obwohl ich müde bin, lerne ich.
Ich bin müde. Trotzdem lerne ich.
“dennoch” means the same thing, but it's more formal, especially in writing.
Don't mix them up: “trotz” + genitive (trotz des Regens = despite the rain), “trotzdem” (even so), “obwohl” (although). Three words, three different constructions.
3. auch wenn / selbst wenn = even if
For a hypothetical or stronger concession:
Even if I had time, I wouldn't come.

After “auch wenn / selbst wenn” the main clause does NOT necessarily start with the verb: “Auch wenn es regnet, wir gehen trotzdem!” is accepted in speech. In writing, use the normal order: “…, gehen wir trotzdem.”
4. How to take the floor in a discussion
Darf ich etwas dazu sagen? / Ich möchte gern etwas sagen.
Darf ich etwas ergänzen? / Dazu möchte ich noch sagen, …
Ihr Einwand ist berechtigt, aber … / Da haben Sie recht, trotzdem …
Ich hätte einen Vorschlag: … / Wie wäre es, wenn …?
Even if it's expensive, we should do it.
I'm tired. Even so, I'm studying.
It's cold. Even so, we're going out.
Although I'm ill, I'm going to work.

The hall of the primary school on Kastanienallee was fuller that Tuesday evening than it had been for years. More than two hundred people sat on little children's chairs or stood along the walls, under the colourful drawings of Year 3. It smelt of gym and wet jackets, because it had been raining outside since midday. Although the meeting wasn't due to start till seven, the first people had arrived at six already, with Thermos flasks and placards. One said in a child's handwriting: “Save our chestnut trees!” Another, in adult handwriting: “Accessibility now!” The street was divided.

Because the problem was real. At the stop in front of number twenty-nine you had to climb two high steps to get onto the tram. For wheelchair users it was impossible, for parents with heavy pushchairs, for old people with bad knees it was dangerous. Ludwig knew that better than anyone. Since he had moved to the ground floor, he almost never took the tram any more, although he had loved it all his life. The steps had become too high. Even so, he was now sitting in the front row, with Susanne beside him, who had come specially from Hanover, and he was against the felling. “I know it's a contradiction,” he told her quietly. “But a man is allowed to be contradictory when he's eighty-three.”

Susanne squeezed his hand. Since the move she had been to Berlin twice more, each time for a weekend, each time with a cake from Hanover that she held on her lap on the train, and each time she had sat in the armchair by the window and talked to Ludwig about Ingrid. They had discovered that Ingrid had said the same sentences to both of them, twenty years apart: “You learn from mistakes. From fear you learn nothing.” Susanne had written the sentence on the wall of her classroom in Hanover. Ludwig had never written it down. He had simply heard it every day.

The discussion lasted two hours. Mrs Krause from the district council, a calm woman with short grey hair and endless patience, explained everything three times: the leaf miner moth, the roots, the expert report, the costs. A young mother with twins in a pushchair said that every morning she had to walk to the next stop, because she couldn't get on at this one. A man in a wheelchair said he had lived on the street for twenty years and had never taken the tram from outside his own house. The hall went quiet when he said that. Although many loved the trees, they all suddenly understood that this wasn't about trees against people, but about people against people. And nobody wanted that.

Then Ludwig stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick, and asked to speak. “For forty years I stopped at this stop,” he said. “With the number 46, then with the M1. I saw thousands of people get on. And I saw old people pulling themselves up by the handrail, mothers lifting their pushchairs, young people helping without being asked. Back then I thought that was normal. That's Berlin. But it isn't true. Although I love the trees, I can't be against a stop where even I can't get on any more. That would be dishonest.”

Then came Lena's suggestion. And then something happened that nobody had expected. Right at the back of the hall, a little girl climbed onto a chair so that people could see her. It was Elif, the youngest of the Yilmaz family, eight years old by now. She was holding a shiny brown conker, high above her head, like a treasure.
I found this one in the autumn under the big tree in the courtyard. I put it in a flowerpot. And now a green leaf is already coming out. Although it's cold outside. I can give it. For the street.

The whole hall turned round. Elif's father, Mr Yilmaz, went red and wanted to get his daughter down from the chair, but Mrs Krause raised her hand. “Let her be,” she said. “Come to the front, please.” And Elif walked across the whole hall, between chairs and wet jackets, with the conker in her hand, and put it on the table in front of Mrs Krause, next to the expert report and the plans. Mrs Krause looked at the conker for a long time. Then she took off her glasses.

The hall was now so quiet that you could hear the rain on the roof. Elif stood by the table and waited, with her hands behind her back, like at school. Jakob, who was standing at the back by the wall, whispered to Mara: “She's in my class. Last week she gave a talk about chestnut trees. Five minutes, without notes. I didn't know she spoke so seriously.” Mara smiled. “Children always speak seriously,” she whispered back. “It's only grown-ups who forget that.”

I've worked at the district council for twenty-three years. I've been to a lot of residents' meetings. Most of the time people shout and in the end everyone is unhappy. Nevertheless, I enjoy this job, for evenings like this one. I propose the following: the old trees will be felled in the autumn, not before, so that the children can collect conkers one more time. The stop will be rebuilt by the spring. And the new trees will come from that courtyard. Who is in favour?

Two hundred hands went up. The young mother with the twins. The man in the wheelchair, who was laughing. The children with the “Save our chestnut trees!” placards. Mr Yilmaz, who was still red, but now with pride. And in the front row Ludwig, who raised his hand higher than everyone else, although his shoulder hurt. Unanimously. Mrs Krause said later that in twenty-three years she had only seen that twice.

After the vote many people came up to Elif to congratulate her. The man in the wheelchair gave her a council pen, which he had got from Mrs Krause. The mother with the twins asked whether her children could help with the planting. And Mrs Krause took the conker with the green leaf and gave it back to Elif. “Look after it,” she said. “In the autumn it will be the first new tree on Kastanienallee. With your name on a little plaque.” Elif nodded very seriously and held the flowerpot tightly with both hands all the way home.

On the way home, under Susanne's umbrella, Ludwig asked her what was happening with Mirko. Susanne had called the day after the move, he knew that, but she hadn't said anything since. She stopped under one of the old chestnut trees, whose branches gleamed in the rain. “It was him,” she said. “He knew straight away who I was. He said: the one with the plaits. And then he didn't say anything for three minutes. I thought the line had gone dead.” She laughed quietly. “He's a viola player in the orchestra of the Dresden State Opera. He has two grown-up sons and has been a widower for four years. In May he's playing in Berlin. At the Konzerthaus. He asked me if I'd come.”

Ludwig stopped beside her and looked up at the chestnut tree. “You know,” he said, “when I was young, I thought life was a straight line, like a tram route. From one terminus to the other. But it isn't true. It's more like the Ring line. You keep passing the same stops. Only each time you're a different person.”
Even though I'm married? Even though forty-two years have gone by? Even though I'm afraid he'll be completely different from how I remember him?

She was silent for a moment. The rain drummed on the umbrella. Above them, in the old branches that would fall in the autumn, a blackbird sat and sang, although it was evening and raining. “Yes,” said Susanne. “Even so. I'm coming. And my husband is coming too. He said he finally wants to meet the man who played the guitar so badly that his wife couldn't forget him for forty-two years.” Ludwig laughed so loudly that the blackbird flew off. “Your husband,” he said, “I like him more and more.”
